newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's UDF gets political support for reform.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's UDF gets political support for reform.

text.p: Bulgaria's main political forces gave broad support on Tuesday to a programme devised by the victorious party in Saturday's elections to lead the country out of crisis.
After talks with the Union of Democratic Forces, the other parties to be represented in the new parliament said they supported the principles of its anti-crisis programme.

The UDF's priorities are carrying out reforms agreed with the International Monetary Fund, fighting organised crime and corruption, opening secret police files on public figures, and bringing Bulgaria into the European Union and NATO.

"In general we agree with the idea for a common declaration on the main principles for finding a way out of the crisis," Georgi Parvanov, leader of the former ruling Socialists, told reporters after meeting UDF leader Ivan Kostov.
He said the Socialists, who were ousted by mass protests in February, supported steps to stabilise the economy and fight crime, but opposed Bulgaria's application to join NATO.
The Socialists, whose failure to launch reforms is blamed for the country's economic near-collapse, will hold 57 seats in the new 240-seat parliament as against 137 for the UDF and its allies.

The UDF won its strongest backing from the small Euroleft coalition, formed by Socialist dissidents, which is expected to play a major role in the new parliament due to its good political relations with both the UDF and its former Socialist associates. It will have 14 seats.
"We agree with all points proposed by the UDF and will support the UDF's anti-crisis declaration in parliament," said Euroleft leader Alexander Tomov.
"It should be understood that the country is really in a very dangerous situation and a minimum national consensus is needed -- so we are giving our share of it," he added.
Tomov said the Euroleft backed the economic stabilisation measures and foreign policy goals of the UDF, but he saw no need for the movement to seek a post in any coalition cabinet.

Both the Socialist Party and the Euroleft expressed concern about the social cost of the reform. The Euroleft said they would propose an additional text in the declaration to guarantee social welfare benefits for the poor.

The Union for National Salvation (UNS), a small parliamentary group which includes the Turkish minority Movement for Rights and Freedoms and monarchist parties seeking the return of exiled King Simeon, said they also broadly supported the UDF.
Even the potentially explosive question of opening communist-era secret police files on supreme court judges and politicians met no objections.
"We support the UDF proposal for opening the files as we have to put an end once and for all to lies and compromises," said UNS co-chairman Alexander Karakachanov.
The Euroleft also voiced their support and the Socialists said they had nothing to fear.

The UDF won an absolute majority in parliament in Saturday's polls and has no constitutional need for other parties' support. But it wants a broad consensus for its potentially painful economic policies.
